reviews.review: A refreshing idea.
This game shows very well what the consequences can be when the privacy of ordinary people is violated.

I really had high hopes for this game, you know? Unfortunately, it didn't quite hit the mark for me. The pace felt a bit sluggish, like waiting for water to boil. And the user interface? Well, let's just say it took a bit of getting used to – kind of like figuring out a new gadget.

Then there's this thing with the HQ, where you're left second-guessing whether they'll appreciate your findings or not. It's like trying to read someone's mind without the manual.

Now, don't get me wrong, if you're into diving deep into lore and soaking up every detail, this game might be right up your alley. But for someone like me, who prefers a bit more action-packed gameplay, it didn't quite scratch the itch.

Interesting focus on the concepts of security and privacy. Narrative remains intriguing throughout and you do feel involved. A unique experience that plays on the norms of social media in our everyday lives.

It can be a bit boring, but if you are into reading a lot then it's nice.

All in all a decent game, I had played it once before having not read Orwell's literary classic and also having much less knowledge on political matters. Replaying it now after having read 1984 and also after having become a socialist, comparing my current run to my previous save was very interesting. My choices went from "liberalism" to "Fuck this, fuck you, fuck them, fuck the police, fuck the establishment, fuck governance, fuck anybody who works for the government, fuck the party, fuck the system, let's burn it all down".

Anywho yeah, recommended.

My first contact with Orwell was back in 2017 when there was some event in my local town square where there were couple of PCs with few games on it for everyone interested to play, and Orwell was one of them. This game actually taught me very very advanced English and I shall ever be so grateful for it.

This game is based on George Orwell's novel "1984" where he mentions the phrase "Big Brother" for the first time. I've never read it but after playing both games [yes there is a second one] I think I just might. Basically it means that you're being spied on all the time. I could describe and explain what "ORWELL" really stands for but that would be a huge spoiler and nobody wants that, right? It is very political, but if I got to play it, a person who knows jack crap about politics, everyone can play it.
If you've never played it before, the average play time is around 4-5 hours, but once you get to do more playthroughs in it can be done in little over 2 hours. I also really liked the low-poly design of the pictures, it really adds to the overall graphics experience.

What was a bad move in my opinion was the fact that you're not actually doing any research on your own, the game automatically highlights the important "datachunks" for you to upload to a corresponding profile. But on the other hand I can imagine how difficult it would have to be for the developers to implement this function. If everyone would put there even just slightly different things it would be a mess. But it's a nice thought to think about.

If you're interested in politics or simply want to improve your English, play this game. I'm pretty sure you will have to translate every third word or so because like I said, it is very professionally written but that's the beauty of it.

If you're a fan of text based adventures, and interested in the ever increasing amounts of surveillance and government interference in your daily lives, Orwell may be the game for you!

Just be wary its a lot, A LOT, of reading, and the pacing can be a little cripplingly slow at times, and you may wonder, just what the hell am I doing, but then, the drama will getcha good.

I'm kind of in between on the whole Should I recommend, should I not recommend this game, its got a story, however I personally got bored reading it. Which caused me to lose interest by the second act, and for replay reasoning I found the pace of the game to be undesirable.

That being said, if you acquire it in a bundle Its a decent story (I'd value this game somewhere between 2-10$). Just need a little more action, or even freedom of discovery without "Symes" constantly adding his unnecessary two cents. Its like being on a rail, or playing an RPG that claims its open world but forces you down a single path.

I really wanted to like this game. Unfortunately the pace is unbearably slow, the UI is unintuitive at parts/annoying, and the "guessing game" on whether the HQ will understand why you may have found something valuable or not just reminded me of a frustrating homework assignment.

Orwell, developed by Osmotic Studios, is a thought-provoking narrative-driven game that immerses players in the unsettling world of government surveillance and ethical dilemmas. Set in the fictional nation of The Nation, the game challenges players to navigate a web of information to uncover the truth while confronting the consequences of their actions.

The premise of Orwell is both intriguing and timely. As a government operative, you are tasked with utilizing the Orwell system to sift through personal data, online communications, and various sources to identify potential threats to national security. The game's central theme revolves around the ethical implications of mass surveillance, forcing players to question the balance between security and privacy.

The gameplay mechanics of Orwell are unique and engaging. Players assume the role of an investigator who must carefully select and analyze information, deciding what to upload to the Orwell system. This decision-making process is a double-edged sword, as the consequences of the information you choose to gather and share can significantly impact the lives of the characters in the narrative.

The narrative unfolds dynamically based on the player's choices, offering multiple branching paths and various possible outcomes. The writing is compelling, creating a sense of urgency and moral complexity that keeps players invested in the unfolding story. The characters are well-developed, and their reactions to your investigative choices add layers of depth to the overall experience.

Visually, Orwell adopts a minimalist yet effective aesthetic. The user interface of the Orwell system is sleek and intuitive, enhancing the immersion into the surveillance theme. The subdued color palette contributes to the game's serious tone and complements the narrative's tension and suspense.

One of Orwell's strengths is its ability to provoke self-reflection. The game confronts players with ethical dilemmas, forcing them to grapple with the consequences of their choices in the pursuit of justice. The sense of moral ambiguity adds a layer of complexity that elevates Orwell beyond a mere detective game.

While Orwell excels in many aspects, it may not appeal to those seeking traditional gameplay mechanics or action-oriented experiences. The deliberate pace and emphasis on narrative choices might not resonate with players who prefer more fast-paced gameplay.

In conclusion, Orwell is a captivating exploration of surveillance, morality, and consequence. Its unique gameplay mechanics and thought-provoking narrative make it a standout experience for those who appreciate story-driven games that challenge both intellect and ethics. Despite its specific appeal, Orwell succeeds in delivering an immersive and impactful journey into the moral gray areas of surveillance society.

I am personally a big fan of satirical works and 1984 and Animal Farm by George Orwell fit right into the category. So when I found a game called Orwell, I instantly bought it. Is this like the source material? No. 

You are a government worker who just got their job due to a new bill that is passed allowing people's data to be looked over (FBI style) and flag people as "potentially dangerous" (kind of like an FBI watchlist).

This game challenges your ability to read people based on a small amount of information given to you. The evidence you choose to process actually affects the lives of the NPCs - from possibly getting doxxed to a full blown shootout - things you can prevent only if you go about everything with discretion and maybe even empathy. This game will make you question your decisions, even if they were correct. 

I personally loved this game, but I can see why some people might not like it. Be warned, there are some very political topics that are discussed. If anyone wants a more in depth review with some spoilers, I might get bored enough for a community blog post.

The story itself isn't very interesting either. Everything is annoyingly generic. For most of the game you can barely figure out what it was that the suspects were actually protesting about. Twists don't make much sense either, and aren't nearly as impressive when you had to do zero work to uncover them. Interesting idea, and definitely innovative as far as visual novels go, but that's all this is... another visual novel masquerading as an adventure game. You don't have to play hours and hours of this to figure out that your choices might provide some slight deviations in the story, but ultimately it's a very narrow path.

There is no adventure here, there are no puzzles.

The interactivity involves dragging across auto-highlighted data you "discover" to build a profile, as well as other profiles connecting to your primary suspect... all from static articles/reports/etc. and active chat sessions that you monitor. No reading through and figuring out what data has actual value the way it is done in the real world. You can read it all, but that isn't really necessary... just skim and speed click your way ahead and you can push the story forward. Feel like you're stuck, something that hasn't been done will remain "starred", so you can go back to that article or whatever and the game will what to do.

Policing/Defense/Military/Whatever-Agency surveillance staff that perform these profile building intelligence jobs and put together these profiles... it's an interesting concept that could have been turned into a fascinating text heavy game that required minimal computing resources or HDD footprint... but the NPC that is effectively your handler guides you the whole way, further holding your hand on top of the highlighted text/data that tells you that you can do something.

That completely kills any mental engagement on a gaming level. You are simply a consumer of a story, which is fine... but that's not a game. That's an interactive short story, or an animated slide show/film/something... not a game.

Steam needs to enforce some sort of standard for the tags to many of these types of "games"... your choices don't really matter here. And a politically themed visual novel that constantly tells you and shows you what to do... that does not qualify as being a "sim". You do not need to "think" when you play Orwell, just obey orders and click where you are allowed to click... you could almost mistake it for a poetic and poignant Orwellian statement on its own existence as a "game"...  but it's not. It really is not.

Overall I liked this game for what it is - it plays mostly like a visual novel with some choice making involved. I would note that I consider this game to play out like a VN, not a detective-work brain scratcher puzzle game. The speculation is fun, but there's no strong deduction decision making really required from the player in order to reach the big end-game truth. 

+ I liked the fact that some decisions the player makes are impactful/referenced by the characters. Not everything the player does has an impact, but when it is referenced in-game it is quite good. 
+ Being able to control what information Orwell receives is a fun gameplay mechanic, it feels like you have agency over the program (to some extent). 
+ The way the player is involved in Orwell is explained in-narrative, so it feels like you as the player are directly engaging in the Orwell program. I thought it was creative and enjoyable immersion-wise.

- Replaying chapters to 100% achievements and make different choices is TEDIOUS - you have to sit through long calls/chatrooms even at the fastest speed they take a long time. When I was achievement hunting I would go on my phone while waiting for the call to finish. 
- I had a glitch where Orwell would keep taking me to the "dating website" profile at random times when I was trying to open other links and pages. I assumed this was a feature [spoiler] like Initiate trying to distract me [/spoiler] but upon further playthroughs it seems to be a bug.
- The endings feel abrupt, I enjoyed the game greatly up until that point. The process of the game is more satisfying than the outcome imo.
